extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in science communication, press officers, science journalists, and academics studying media and health communication
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for identifying and measuring exaggeration in academic press releases and associated health news by comparing press releases and news items to their underlying peer‑reviewed articles, focusing on advice, causal claims, and human inference from non‑human studies, and on news uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration in advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases or news contain stronger or additional advice compared to the associated peer‑reviewed article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined by comparing press releases and news to their associated journal articles to identify when advice goes beyond what the article supports. The replication study found that the association between news and press releases did not replicate for advice exaggeration (i.e., advice exaggeration in press releases did not reliably predict advice exaggeration in news in this cohort).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerated causal claims (claims of causality from correlational evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases or news assert causal relationships despite the underlying peer‑reviewed article providing only correlational evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalised by comparing the strength/type of causal language in press releases/news to that in the journal article. The study reports that the association between news and press releases did replicate for causal claims, indicating that stronger causal language in press releases is associated with stronger causal language in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human inference from non‑human studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases or news infer effects in humans from studies conducted on non‑human samples (e.g., animal or in vitro studies), beyond what the article supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by checking whether press release/news make human‑directed claims that are not warranted by the non‑human evidence in the peer‑reviewed article. The study found the association between press releases and news replicated for this category, and noted lower base exaggeration rates for this type—possibly reflecting the UK Concordat on Openness on Animal Research.

rubrics_metrics.name: News uptake for exaggerated press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether press releases that contain exaggerated statements attract more news coverage than non‑exaggerated press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessed by comparing rates of news pickup for press releases classified as exaggerated versus not exaggerated. The study found no evidence that exaggerated press releases attracted significantly more news, consistent with previous results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association between press release statement strength and news statement strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the strength of statements in news items corresponds to the strength of statements in the associated press releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overall conclusion: 'the strength of news statements is normally associated with the strength of press release statements,' i.e., stronger claims in press releases tend to be mirrored by stronger claims in news, even though exaggeration does not appear to increase news uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological standard: comparison to peer‑reviewed article
rubrics_metrics.description: Define and detect exaggeration by comparing press releases and news content directly to the content of the associated peer‑reviewed journal article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comparison forms the basis for classifying exaggeration across the categories (advice, causal claims, human inference). The paper uses this approach on a cohort of press releases and news items from UK universities (2014–2015) as a replication of prior work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base exaggeration rates by category
rubrics_metrics.description: The baseline frequency of exaggeration differs by category (advice, causal claims, human inference), with some categories showing lower rates of exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study reports that base exaggeration rates were lower for human inference from non‑human studies, possibly influenced by policy environment (e.g., Concordat on Openness on Animal Research in the UK). These baseline rates are relevant when interpreting associations and news uptake analyses.
